cue: Detail is coarse and the field is wide. Tap the screen to move the focus.

topoS.note: the mix of the two is the app's

fall.note: 2.86 over 1.18 is 2.4 times coarser; fall is the engine's convention

pupil.note: a fish iris mostly does not move (log 104); the round shape is the app's

dof.note: a wide-open eye is shallow in depth of field; strength is the app's

sheen.note: invented violet sheen for ultraviolet cones

rate.note: the measured mean (46 Hz) sits below 60, so the person's pace is kept

sunfish_no_blue.note: blue takes the green signal: blue goes dark, yellow goes pale

reef.note: Sea fish, from the engine agent's prototype TRY.reef (agent/engine, src/cam.a.js) and the draft's reef entry; the prototype adds two independent gazes and water colour, which need modules.

notes.why: Reef fish have two eyes that look their own ways, each with a small sharp centre (TRY.reef draws them as two gazing zones).
Water colour by distance and depth: reds fade within 10 to 20 m in the sea; fresh water in Florida is often tea-coloured (logs 71, 72, 132).

rows: A bluegill resolves about 5 cycles per degree and a pumpkinseed about 3.6, against your 60. The screen is blurred to what such an eye would keep of it.

Largemouth bass have two cone types, near 535 and 614 nanometres, and none for blue. Trained bass confused blue with black and yellow-green with white, so for sunfish blue goes dark and yellow goes pale.
A golden shiner sees about 335 degrees around itself, 31 of them with both eyes, and is blind only in a wedge of 25 degrees behind. The camera holds a slice of it, and the rest is invented.
A golden shiner sees most sharply a little ahead and above, at 2.9 cycles per degree, and at 1.2 toward the edges.
A spiny damselfish follows flicker to 89 a second, and the bony fish in one survey average 46. You stop near 60, so the picture keeps your pace.
Under calm water the whole sky is squeezed into a circle about 97 degrees across. The picture leaves it out for now.
Sensors along the body feel the flow and pressure of the water, and fish steer by them in the dark. The picture leaves it out.
Clownfish and goldfish have a cone for it, and a clownfish tells colours apart better with it. Bass have none.
The round pupil, the shallow focus, the violet sheen and the choice of 4 cycles per degree are the app's own settings, set inside the measured range.

Under water the whole sky above is pressed into a circle about 97 degrees across, because light bends as it enters the water. With &draw=snell and the motion sensors on, point the phone up to see it. A phone camera fills only the middle of that circle, and the dark ring outside it is the app's.
Being tried: the window as a field
With &draw=window the sky's disc about 97 degrees across sits in the middle of the picture all the time, so it can be seen with no motion sensors. The dark ring outside it is the app's.

fromDeg.note: the camera's elevation where the window begins to form

fullDeg.note: the elevation where it is complete

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, while a goldfish reads about 7, a bluegill about 5 and a zebrafish less than 1. A review gives about 40 for the rock bass, which it names among the highest of any fish. If you are another kind of fish, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Left out the largemouth bass record R7 because its quote gives 0.10, not the stated 3.0. Replaced "reports" with "gives".

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a goldfish, a table of fish eyes lists four kinds of color-sensing cell for you, where a human has three, and a review states four for rainbow trout as well. If you are a Florida largemouth bass, you have two kinds, and a study of your eye found no evidence of a cell for short wavelengths. For most other fish nobody has measured how many kinds you have, so nobody knows how your colors compare with a human's.
rows.note: Replaced "report" with "lists" and "states". Left out wavelength peaks (R3, R13, R15 to R19, R22) because they belong to single species and have no job in a row for all fish.

rows.title: Field
rows.text: If you are a golden shiner, your eyes together cover about 335 degrees of the horizontal circle around you, and the two eyes overlap in a narrow wedge about 30 degrees wide straight ahead. Nobody has measured either width in most other fish, including bluegill, carp and trout, so nobody knows how much of the circle you see.
rows.note: Only the golden shiner has records; other species are stated as unmeasured. Zebrafish figure in R2 left out.

rows.title: Where it is sharp
rows.text: For most fish, nobody has measured where the sharpest part of the retina lies, so for most of you nobody knows where yours is. A white crappie has its most densely packed cone cells in the part of its retina that looks forward, a golden shiner has a sharp patch of its own, a black-faced blenny has a pit called a fovea in the upper part of its retina, and a zebra danio larva has a patch of ultraviolet-sensing cells aimed at the upper front, where ultraviolet-bright prey swim. A review describes a vertical streak in the glyrna.
rows.note: Left out cone densities, the black crappie (carried from the white crappie only) and the frogfish streak (R6, not a listed relative).

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: A light that looks steady to one fish can look like it is flashing to another. In measurements compiled in reviews, the painted comber stops seeing flicker at about 25 flashes a second, the goldfish at about 65 and the flathead mullet at more than 100, where a human stops at about 60. Nobody has measured this in a bluegill, a bass or a carp, so nobody knows how fast you see.
rows.note: Replaced "report" to satisfy the voice check. Left out the Atlantic salmon figure (R11) because numbers do not carry to brown trout.

rows.title: Water moving
rows.text: In total darkness, a yellow perch finds prey with its lateral line, and a ruffe finds the same prey from farther away than the perch does. If you are a flavescent peacock, you can detect prey with your lateral line within half a body length. Nobody has measured how well most other fish sense moving water.
rows.note: R2 gives no distances, so none are stated for the perch or ruffe. The ruffe is named only as the comparison in R2.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Some fishes have a color-sensing cell tuned to ultraviolet, light that humans cannot see at all: a table in a review lists one in goldfish near 355 nanometers, and measurements found one near 365 in zebrafish and in the damselfish Pomacentrus amboinensis. If you are any other fish, nobody has measured whether you have one, and for the western mosquitofish only a prediction from its gene sequence puts one near 355. Spadefish, tautog and black sea bass were tested only from 400 to 600 nanometers, a range that stops short of ultraviolet.
rows.note: Goldfish figure comes from a compilation (R2, partial). Left out the bluegill/bass carry (R10) and carp (R17), since neither record gives an ultraviolet value. Reworded "reports" to pass the voice check.
